title: What Happens When Molecules Meet?
bullets: Organic molecules react to change their shapes and jobs.
A molecule can swap one piece for another piece.
This swap reaction is called nucleophilic substitution.
A molecule can also lose pieces to make double bonds.
This loss reaction is called elimination.
notes: Welcome to organic mechanisms. Today we explore substitution and elimination.

title: Why It Matters: Real Uses of These Reactions
bullets: Alkyl halides are used as solvents, anesthetics, and refrigerants.
Alcohols are used as fuels, solvents, and antiseptics.
Chemists use these reactions to build bigger molecules.
The wrong reaction gives a different product, such as an alkene.
By the end, you will predict which path wins.
notes: Uses come from wiki/index.md (Why It Matters), fed by Wade sections 6-3 and 10-5.

title: Key Vocabulary: The Reaction Team
bullets: Substrate: The main carbon molecule that undergoes the reaction.
Leaving Group (LG): A part that departs with bond electrons.
Nucleophile: An electron-rich atom that attacks a positive carbon.
Base: A molecule that removes a hydrogen proton from carbon.
notes: These four players appear in all substitution and elimination reactions.

title: Key Vocabulary: Carbon Crowding (1°, 2°, 3°)
bullets: Carbons are named by how many other carbons touch them.
Primary (1°): The reactive carbon touches only one other carbon.
Secondary (2°): The reactive carbon touches two other carbons.
Tertiary (3°): The reactive carbon touches three other carbons.
Tertiary carbons are very crowded, like a packed room.
notes: Steric crowding determines which pathway a molecule can take.

title: SN2: One Step, Backside Attack
bullets: SN2 means Substitution Nucleophilic Bimolecular.
The reaction takes place in one fast, concerted step.
The nucleophile attacks the back of the reactive carbon.
The leaving group gets pushed out at the same time.
Reaction speed depends on both substrate and nucleophile: Rate = k[substrate][Nu].
notes: Notice there is no waiting and no intermediate in SN2.

title: SN2: The Umbrella Flip and Open Paths
bullets: The backside attack turns the molecule inside out.
This 3D shape flip is called Walden inversion.
Crowded carbons block the nucleophile from attacking.
Speed order: Methyl > Primary (1°) > Secondary (2°). Tertiary (3°) is blocked.
Polar aprotic solvents like acetone speed up SN2.
notes: Like an umbrella blown inside out on a windy day, configuration inverts.

title: SN1: Break First, Attach Later
bullets: SN1 means Substitution Nucleophilic Unimolecular.
The reaction happens in two separate steps.
A carbocation is a flat carbon with a positive charge.
Step 1 (slow): The leaving group leaves and a carbocation forms.
Reaction speed depends only on the substrate: Rate = k[substrate].
notes: Because ionization is the slow step, nucleophile concentration does not matter.

title: SN1: Flat Intermediate and Mixed Products
bullets: Step 2: The nucleophile attacks the flat carbocation (fast step).
The nucleophile can attack from the top or the bottom.
Attacking both faces gives a 50:50 mixture called racemization.
Tertiary (3°) carbons make the most stable carbocations.
Polar protic solvents like water help the leaving group depart.
notes: Planar geometry removes top and bottom differences, leading to racemization.

title: E2: The One-Step Team Elimination
bullets: E2 means Elimination Bimolecular.
It forms a carbon-carbon double bond (alkene) in one step.
A strong base pulls off a neighboring beta-hydrogen.
At the same time, the leaving group leaves.
Speed depends on both substrate and base: Rate = k[substrate][base].
notes: All three bond changes occur together in a single transition state.

title: E2: The Opposite Line and Base Size
bullets: The hydrogen and the leaving group must sit on opposite sides.
Anti-periplanar means the two groups sit 180° apart.
A small base gives the more stable alkene (Zaitsev rule).
A bulky base gives the less crowded alkene (Hofmann rule).
Adding heat strongly favors E2 over substitution.
notes: Bulky bases like KOtBu cannot reach inside, so they pick the outer hydrogen.

title: E1: Two Steps to a Double Bond
bullets: E1 means Elimination Unimolecular.
Step 1: The leaving group falls off, making a carbocation.
Step 2: A weak base removes a beta-hydrogen.
The electrons collapse to form a double bond (alkene).
E1 usually gives the most substituted alkene (Zaitsev product).
notes: E1 shares Step 1 with SN1. High heat favors E1 over SN1.

title: Comparison: The Four Pathways Side by Side
bullets: SN2: 1 step, backside swap, prefers uncrowded 1° carbons.
SN1: 2 steps, carbocation swap, prefers crowded 3° carbons.
E2: 1 step, strong base elimination, anti-periplanar 180° geometry.
E1: 2 steps, weak base elimination, needs high heat.
notes: Remember: '2' mechanisms take 1 step, and '1' mechanisms take 2 steps.

title: How to Choose: The 3-Step Decision Tree
bullets: Step 1: Check carbon crowding (1° favors SN2; 3° is too crowded for SN2).
Step 2: Check reagent strength (Strong = SN2 or E2; Weak = SN1 or E1).
Step 3: Check temperature (high heat favors elimination).
Follow these three steps to predict the correct product.
notes: This simple 3-step logic solves almost every introductory exam problem.

title: Practice: Test Your Prediction Skills
bullets: 1-bromobutane (1°) with strong cyanide nucleophile → SN2 substitution.
2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3°) with strong ethoxide base plus heat → E2 alkene.
2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3°) with neutral water at room temp → SN1 alcohol.
Notice how temperature and reagent strength steer the outcome.
notes: Work through these examples using the 3-step decision tree.

title: Summary: Your Reaction Cheat Sheet
bullets: Bimolecular (2) reactions happen in a single concerted step.
Unimolecular (1) reactions form a flat carbocation intermediate.
Strong bases favor E2, while weak reagents allow carbocations.
High temperature acts as a switch to produce alkenes.
You now understand SN1, SN2, E1, and E2 mechanisms!
notes: Congratulations! You have mastered the core mechanisms of organic chemistry.
